slides.text: High in the cloud-piercing spire of St. Jude of the Crags hangs the Vesper Bell, cast from meteoric bronze before the first king was crowned. No rope is tied to its yoke. It rings on its own exactly twenty-four hours before a catastrophe strikes the valley below—a low, mournful iron dirge for floods, a jagged clanging for war.

Because the sound drives hearing men mad with dread, only deaf monks are chosen to sweep the belfry and read the vibrations through the soles of their bare feet. For fifty years, Brother Lucian had felt only warnings of sorrow trembling through the flagstones, dutifully lighting the signal beacons so the villagers could flee.

Then, in the dead of a starless winter when famine had brought the valley to its knees, the great bell swung so violently it cracked the masonry. Lucian pressed his palms against the freezing bronze and wept—not from terror, but because for the first time in a thousand years, the metal was humming the unmistakable, rhythmic cadence of a wedding march and spring rain.
